Hi everyone, I'm Jason, based in Los Alamos, NM.

First and foremost, as a computer scientist, thank you for all of your work on the Lean framework. It is truly amazing to work with.

My background is in computer science and supporting particle physics. Recently, I was running some numerical optimization experiments on the Nyman-Beurling continuous formulation of the Riemann Hypothesis, seeing if I could use higher-dimensional algebras (like Octonions) as a data structure to block-diagonalize the Gram matrix of fractional parts.

When the numerical optimizer rejected my geometric buckets and instead organically separated the primes from the semiprimes (essentially colliding head-first with Selberg's parity barrier), I realized I had stumbled into deep analytic number theory and needed to stop guessing and start formalizing.

That led to a rather dedicated sprint working on a large-scale Lean 4 formalization project, mapping out the analytic and spectral dependencies of RH (specifically the Nyman-Beurling criterion and the Lagarias/Robin inequalities). I'm focused heavily on proof architecture—separating the discrete arithmetic from the  functional analysis into domain-isolated axioms. I also decided to ask Claude to build up a Next.js visualizer for the RH dependency tree.

Because I am a systems architect and not a Lean expert, I relied heavily on an AI workflow: I used Gemini Advanced (Deep Think) as a mathematical theorist to bounce ideas off of, and Claude 4.6 Opus as the coding engineer to wrestle with the compiler.

I'm joining to ask some specific questions (which I'll post over in #maths) about how best to align my project's axiomatic boundaries with Mathlib's ongoing analytic number theory efforts. Looking forward to learning from you all!
